question: Your team runs Claude Code in CI with the -p flag to label new bug reports with a component and a severity. Labels with high field-level confidence are applied without human review. Each week, reviewers check a uniform random 2% sample of these high-confidence labels, and the measured error rate stays low. Developers later find that labels for the small mobile component have shown a new error pattern for weeks. Which change to the weekly audit best supports ongoing error rate measurement and detection of new error patterns?

options.text: Have reviewers check only the labels whose confidence scores sit just above the automation threshold, because these borderline labels are the most likely to contain errors.
options.reason: This sample is not random across the high-confidence labels. Errors among the highest-confidence labels and new error patterns in small segments stay unmeasured, which the guide's stratified random sampling is meant to catch.

options.text: Review every mobile label each week, and keep the uniform 2% sample for all other components and fields as before.
options.reason: This fixes only the segment that already failed. The uniform sample still under-samples the other small segments, so the next novel error pattern can stay hidden, unlike with the stratified sampling that the guide recommends.

options.text: Pause the weekly audit for components with a low measured error rate, and move all reviewer time to the mobile component's labels.
options.reason: The guide calls for ongoing error rate measurement of high-confidence extractions. Stopping the audit for most components removes that measurement, so new error patterns there go undetected.

options.text: Stratify the weekly random sample by component and field, so each segment, including small ones like mobile, gets enough reviewed labels to show its own error rate.
options.reason: The guide recommends stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions for ongoing error rate measurement and novel pattern detection. Stratifying makes sure that small segments are sampled often enough to reveal their errors.
